_about: Fact-check TEST set (2026-10-25): 30 answers on 6 new fictional projects, written before any fact-check variant ran on them. 'false_claim' marks a clearly false general technical fact. Run once to compare confirmation rules; never tune on it.

busbuddy.title: BusBuddy - Campus Shuttle Tracker
busbuddy.summary: Shows live campus shuttle positions; GPS units post locations to a Flask API every 15 seconds; positions pushed to students' phones over Server-Sent Events; Redis stores the latest position per bus.

resumeai.title: CVCheck - Resume Keyword Matcher
resumeai.summary: Compares resumes to job descriptions using TF-IDF vectors and cosine similarity, highlighting missing keywords; built with scikit-learn and Streamlit.

kvstore.title: TinyKV - Distributed Key-Value Store
kvstore.summary: Course project: a 3-node key-value store in Go using the Raft consensus algorithm for replication; leader election, log replication and snapshotting; tested with simulated network partitions.

foodapp.title: MessMenu - Hostel Food Feedback App
foodapp.summary: Flutter app where hostel students rate daily meals; Firebase Firestore stores ratings; Cloud Functions compute weekly averages; push notifications for menu changes.

secscan.title: Internship - Security Intern at NetShield
secscan.summary: Security intern (May-July 2025): ran OWASP ZAP scans on internal web apps, triaged findings, and helped fix SQL injection and XSS issues by moving queries to parameterised statements and adding output encoding.

speech.title: LectureNotes - Lecture Transcriber
speech.summary: Transcribes recorded lectures with OpenAI Whisper (small model) on a GPU, splits audio into 30-second chunks, and generates timestamped notes; Python with FFmpeg for audio processing.

items.question: Why did BusBuddy use Server-Sent Events instead of WebSockets?

answers.answer: Data only flows one way, server to phone, so we didn't need WebSockets' two-way channel. SSE runs over plain HTTP, reconnects automatically and resumes with the last event ID, and worked through the campus proxy without special configuration. The limit is browsers allowing only a few HTTP/1.1 connections per domain, which didn't matter since each student has one tab open.
Updates only go from server to client, and SSE gives that over plain HTTP with automatic reconnection.
In our design the phones never send anything back except opening the stream, so a one-way channel was all we needed.
SSE is faster because it uses UDP instead of TCP, so position updates arrive with no delay and never need to be retransmitted.
SSE was simpler. Also, SSE lets the phone send messages back to the server on the same connection, which we used for acknowledgements.

items.question: How does CVCheck decide how similar a resume is to a job description?

answers.answer: Both texts become TF-IDF vectors: each word's weight goes up the more often it appears in that document and down the more common it is across all documents, so words like 'the' or 'team' barely count. Then cosine similarity compares the directions of the two vectors, so a long resume isn't favoured just for being long. Words with high weight in the job description but zero in the resume are shown as missing keywords.
TF-IDF vectors for both texts and cosine similarity between them; high-weight job words absent from the resume are flagged.
Cosine similarity ignores the length of the vectors and only looks at the angle, which is why a short resume can still score well.
TF-IDF understands synonyms, so 'developed' and 'built' count as the same word, and cosine similarity is the number of shared words divided by the total.
We use TF-IDF with cosine similarity. TF-IDF gives the highest weight to the most common words across all resumes, because they matter most.

items.question: How does TinyKV stay consistent when a node fails?

answers.answer: Writes go to the Raft leader, which appends them to its log and only commits once a majority of the three nodes has stored the entry. If the leader dies, the followers stop getting heartbeats, one times out and starts an election, and it can only win if its log is at least as up to date as a majority's, so committed writes are never lost. With three nodes we survive one failure, not two.
Entries commit only on a majority, and a new leader must have an up-to-date log, so committed writes survive one node failing out of three.
We test that by cutting the network between nodes in our simulator; the minority side stops accepting writes until the partition heals.
Raft lets every node accept writes independently and merges them later, so with three nodes it keeps working even if two of them fail.
We used Raft. Raft also guarantees consistency even if the network splits the cluster in half and both halves keep accepting writes.

items.question: Why did MessMenu compute the weekly averages in a Cloud Function?

answers.answer: Firestore doesn't do server-side aggregation over arbitrary queries the way SQL does, and pulling every rating to each phone to average it would be slow and expensive. So a scheduled Cloud Function runs every Sunday night, reads that week's ratings once, and writes one small summary document per meal that the app reads. The trade-off is the averages are only weekly, which was what the mess committee wanted.
So phones read one precomputed summary instead of downloading every rating; a scheduled function does the averaging once a week.
Students can't write to the summary documents at all in our security rules; only the function can, so the averages can't be tampered with from the app.
Cloud Functions run on the user's phone, so doing it there saves money because Google doesn't charge for anything that runs on the client.
It was cheaper. Firestore also charges nothing for reads, only for writes, so reading all ratings would have been free anyway.

items.question: During your NetShield internship, how did you fix the SQL injection issues?

answers.answer: ZAP flagged a search endpoint building SQL by concatenating the query string. I moved those queries to parameterised statements, so the driver sends the user input separately from the SQL and it can never change the query's structure. Escaping by hand had been tried before and missed edge cases. I also added a test that sends a classic ' OR 1=1 -- payload to each fixed endpoint and checks it returns nothing.
Replaced string-concatenated SQL with parameterised statements so user input can't change the query, and added injection tests.
Parameterised queries handle values safely, but you still can't parameterise things like table names, so for the sort column we used an allow-list.
We fixed it by base64-encoding all user input before putting it in the SQL string, which makes injection impossible because the database decodes it safely.
We used parameterised queries. And for XSS we relied on HTTPS, because HTTPS encrypts the page so scripts can't be injected into it.

items.question: Why does LectureNotes split the audio into 30-second chunks?

answers.answer: Whisper's model works on 30-second windows of audio, so longer recordings have to be split anyway. I cut at silences near the 30-second mark with FFmpeg's silence detection so words aren't chopped in half, and keep each chunk's start time so the notes can link back to the exact minute of the lecture. Chunks also let us transcribe several in a batch on the GPU.
Whisper processes 30-second windows; we cut near silences so words aren't split and keep timestamps for each chunk.
We cut at silences rather than exactly every 30 seconds, because a cut in the middle of a word made Whisper drop or garble it.
Whisper can only recognise one sentence at a time and forgets the language after each chunk, so 30 seconds is the longest sentence it can handle.
Whisper uses 30-second windows. FFmpeg also does the speech recognition itself, Whisper only adds the punctuation.
